title: Who’s Borrowing and Lending in Repo Markets? - Liberty Street Economics
gist: NY Fed primer on private repo markets (about $13.5 trillion outstanding, 40 percent of GDP, 70 percent Treasury-collateralized): hedge funds are the top cash borrowers (about $3 trillion by late 2025, driven by basis trades) and money market funds the top lenders (about $3 trillion by January 2026). Part one of a three-part series; later posts cover microstructure and monetary policy.

insights.claim: The U.S. repo market has roughly $13.5 trillion of agreements outstanding daily, about 40 percent of U.S. GDP, making it a core plumbing layer of the financial system.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Repo stress or rate moves propagate through a market this large; monitor repo rates as a system-wide funding gauge.
insights.quote: Repos are an essential component of the U.S. financial system

insights.claim: About 70 percent of repos are collateralized by U.S. Treasuries and most are overnight, so repo funding is tightly bound to Treasury market conditions and needs constant rollover.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Treasury supply and liquidity shocks transmit directly into short-term funding; overnight maturity means funding can reprice or vanish quickly.

insights.claim: Roughly 60 percent of repos are centrally cleared (35 percent via a central counterparty, 25 percent via a third party) while 40 percent are cleared directly between buyer and seller.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Bilateral share of about 40 percent is the less transparent, less centrally managed part of the market; clearing mandates shift this mix.

insights.claim: Repo rates depend on collateral type, maturity, counterparty, haircut size and clearing method, so there is no single repo rate but a family of segmented rates.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: When reading funding stress, distinguish GC, specific-collateral, cleared and bilateral rates rather than one headline print.

insights.claim: Treasury and federal agency repos are exempt from the Bankruptcy Code's automatic stay, letting cash lenders terminate and sell collateral promptly if the borrower defaults, which has supported repo liquidity and growth.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: The legal safe harbor is a structural reason repo is treated as safe funding; changes to it would reprice repo markets.
insights.locator: Repos can be traced back to the early 20th century

insights.claim: Repo market size and contracting conventions changed markedly in the 1980s after several dealer failures, amid rising and volatile interest rates and growing Treasury debt supply.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Historical precedent that dealer failures reshape repo conventions; useful context for judging how crises could change today's rules.
insights.locator: Repos can be traced back to the early 20th century

themes.theme: Repo motives: funding versus specific securities

insights.claim: A repo has one party borrowing cash and a counterparty that either invests cash for a return or obtains a specific security; the first motive makes repo economically similar to fed funds, Eurodollars or commercial paper, but collateralized.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Repo should be compared to other money-market instruments as the collateralized version; collateral lowers lender risk and rate.

insights.claim: In general collateral (GC) repo the lender accepts any security meeting set criteria, making GC repo a funding market for cash borrowers financing a basket of securities and cash lenders seeking a competitive rate.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: The GC rate is the benchmark for secured funding costs against which specials are measured.

insights.claim: In the worked example a money market fund lends $98 million overnight against Treasuries with a 2 percent haircut and receives $98,009,800 the next day, a 3.6 percent annualized return.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Illustrates that a 3.6 percent annualized overnight repo return is the reference yield MMFs earn on secured cash.
insights.locator: An Example of a Repo Transaction

insights.claim: A security in high demand relative to supply becomes a 'special' and trades at a lower repo rate than GC, because the cash lender seeking the scarce asset forgoes some return.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Rates well below GC signal scarcity or crowded shorts in a specific Treasury; a useful positioning indicator.
insights.locator: Participants may also engage in repo to acquire a specific security

insights.claim: Repo resembles securities lending against cash collateral, differing mainly in that repo uses fixed-income collateral and typically gives the lender no right of early recall.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Explains why special repo rates work as the price of borrowing a specific bond.
insights.locator: Participants may also engage in repo to acquire a specific security

themes.theme: Hedge funds as top cash borrowers

insights.claim: Hedge funds are the largest cash borrowers in private repo markets, using repo for leverage to boost returns.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Hedge fund leverage is a major channel through which repo conditions affect Treasury market stability.
insights.quote: The top cash borrowers in private repo markets are hedge funds.

insights.claim: The Treasury cash-futures basis trade buys a Treasury, sells a Treasury futures contract, and is levered by financing the purchase in repo against the same securities.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Basis-trade unwinds forced by repo funding tightening or margin calls are a known Treasury-market fragility to monitor.

insights.claim: Hedge fund repo borrowing tripled over 2013-23 from $400 billion to $1.5 trillion, then doubled again over the next two years to $3 trillion by late 2025.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Rapid growth in leveraged Treasury financing raises systemic risk if funding conditions or basis spreads turn.
insights.quote: hedge fund borrowing in repo markets tripled over 2013-23

insights.claim: The next three largest repo borrowers (U.S. branches of foreign banks, U.S. depository institutions and REITs) together have borrowed between $800 billion and $1.3 trillion since 2013, far below hedge funds' $3 trillion.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Hedge funds now dominate marginal repo borrowing; other borrower groups are comparatively stable.

themes.theme: Money market funds as top cash lenders

insights.claim: Money market funds are the main cash lenders in repo; their lending rose 90 percent from under $600 billion in January 2013 to $1 trillion in January 2021, then almost tripled to $3 trillion by January 2026.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: MMF inflows are the key supply of repo cash; MMF asset growth and allocation shifts drive repo funding availability and rates.

insights.claim: Repo suits MMFs because it is a short-term investment meeting their regulatory maturity and asset-composition requirements while giving flexibility to manage investor redemptions.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: MMF regulation structurally channels cash into repo, so rule changes or redemption waves shift repo supply.

insights.claim: Hedge funds are the second largest repo lenders despite being net borrowers, lending about $1.3 trillion in late 2025 up from $350 billion in early 2013, to manage cash and liquidity and for collateral transformation.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Hedge funds are on both sides of repo, so gross exposures and interconnectedness exceed net borrowing figures.

insights.claim: GSEs, foreign bank branches and U.S. depository institutions, also key in fed funds, Eurodollar and selected deposits markets, jointly lent $0.6-$1.5 trillion in repo over 2013-25.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Money-market participants move across funding venues, so repo rates are linked to fed funds and Eurodollar conditions.

insights.claim: Repos play a key role in monetary policy implementation and central banks use them in their toolkits; the series' third post is set to cover this.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Repo rates and volumes are a transmission channel for policy and balance-sheet decisions; watch the series' later posts.

insights.claim: Private repo is more complex than fed funds or Eurodollar markets because of a broader, more diverse set of ultimate borrowers and lenders, plus dealers acting as instrumental intermediaries.
insights.speaker: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
insights.so_what: Dealer balance-sheet capacity is a bottleneck between cash lenders and borrowers; the series' second post covers it.

source_meta.author: Gara Afonso, Jun-Davinci Choi, Gonzalo Cisternas, and Will Riordan
